nc_08_amphitheater.blurb: A deep stone bowl crowned by a band of roofs, this wall sits in the Piedmont foothills at Pilot Mountain State Park and is mostly a bolted-line crag. Around two dozen routes share the cliff: the large majority are sport, with a few gear lines and a handful of top-rope setups. Difficulty begins near 5.7 with a small group of easier lines, then bunches up through the 5.10s and 5.11s, and a few 5.12 and 5.13 projects tackle the overhangs. The quartzite is uneven in quality. Expect hot days in summer and plenty of company on weekends.
nc_08_amphitheater.approach: Take the maintained trail from the southwest corner of the top lot, follow the stone steps down into the Three Bears gully, then turn left and walk along the base of the cliff.

nc_west_cliff_main.blurb: The better developed of two cliffs in a small climbing park near Tryon, in the western Carolina foothills. About 25 routes, mostly bolted, with a good number of trad lines and some that double as top ropes, plus a single aid line. Grades sit chiefly between 5.7 and 5.11, with the heaviest concentration around 5.8 to 5.10, so it suits climbers stepping up from the gym as well as those working harder lines. Walls are short, topping out around fifty feet, with big holds and some overhanging jugs. The rock is gneiss that varies from solid to brittle, so test holds. Afternoon sun reaches the cliff, and tree cover keeps it fairly shady in summer.

nc_amphitheater_the.blurb: A big buttress toward the north end of Moore's Wall in Hanging Rock State Park, whose curving faces form a cirque. All of the roughly two dozen routes are trad, running from about 5.6 up to the low 5.11s, with the biggest cluster around 5.10 and a decent spread of moderates in the 5.6 to 5.9 range. Several lines are more than one pitch and need specific descents. The quartzite here leans on friction and slopers more than the neighboring walls do. The sunniest face warms up well on cool days, while the right-hand side stays cooler in summer. An intimidating but rewarding wall.

nc_southeast_face.blurb: The main cliff on Whiteside Mountain in the North Carolina highlands, standing at roughly 4,900 feet. It is a multi-pitch trad wall: most routes run six to ten pitches, with a few aid lines mixed in. The difficulty is stiff, with nearly all the routes in the 5.11 and 5.12 range and only a couple of easier ones. This is serious terrain with long distances between protection, so strong route-finding and gear skills matter. Reaching the base means following the loop trail from the lot, dropping through rhododendron and a gully, then walking left along the cliff line. Most of the harder testpieces here are some of the best known in the region.

nc_comatose_area.blurb: A quieter corner of Rumbling Bald in the Hickory Nut Gorge, above Lake Lure, with views over the water from the cliff base. Of about two dozen routes, nearly all are gear climbs, with just a couple of bolted lines. Difficulty runs from 5.7 to the low 5.11s, but the bulk of the routes fall at 5.10 and below, so it offers plenty for a day at moderate grades. Expect a mix of arching cracks and thin edged faces on gneiss. The approach follows an old road, then a smaller path past a boulder field before contouring left. Fewer people than elsewhere at the Bald, and cooler months are more comfortable.

nc_fin_area_the.blurb: Named for a ridge profile that looks like a dorsal fin, this is the westernmost stretch of Cooks Wall in Hanging Rock State Park, part of the West Walls. It holds one of the biggest clusters of routes at the wall: 24 lines, about two-thirds bolted and the rest trad. Grades run from roughly 5.9 to the low 5.12s, with half of them at 5.11 and a good number at 5.10. The quartzite is a bit weaker here as the cliff starts to break up. Because lines are close together, it works well for a day of mid-grade sport and gear climbing.

nc_04_david_s_castle_wall.blurb: A wall just east of the top of Crowders Mountain, in the state park west of Charlotte, split in two by a tall chimney. There are 23 routes, mostly trad with a handful of bolted lines and some top-rope options. Grades span from fourth-class and easy fifth-class lines up to the low 5.12s, though the largest group sits at 5.10 with a good number at 5.11, so it works for both beginners seeking easy gear routes and stronger climbers. The rock is quartzite. Reach it by following a trail down from the Practice Wall, turning right, and walking around to the chimney.

_skipped.nc_main_wall_the: Sits under a parent area filed as closed to climbing; no page about this wall itself found.
